clue.text: Reckless gamble a feature of theme, when it comes to pointing the finger?

definitions.note: the definition is an activity, apportioning fault to others

indicators.note: something that is a feature of a thing sits within it, so these letters go inside the word theme
reckless means wild and uncontrolled, so the letters of gamble a are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A rash bet that suits the theme of a game of accusations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reckless' makes BLAMEGA and 'feature of' sets it inside. 'Theme' is a wink at the puzzle's own theme, the Jacksons' song Blame It on the Boogie.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the situation where everyone accuses someone else rather than accept responsibility.

clue.text: Painter, after short vacation, to live at home

parts.note: a holiday cut short is hol
to be is to exist or live
someone at home is in

explanation.surface: An artist settles back at home after a brief holiday.
explanation.definitionFit: Hans Holbein the Younger was a German-Swiss portrait artist at the court of Henry VIII.

clue.text: Leave dive showing a moon

definitions.meaning: to stop falling and level off, as a market or plane does when it pulls out of a plunge
to moon is to expose one's backside, so the rear end is displayed

explanation.walkthrough: The second reading is a joke: someone mooning has their behind on show.
explanation.definitionFit: A price that stops sinking has reached its lowest level and levelled off; literally, a backside on display is a bared rump.

clue.text: Tossing this old coin won't make a difference

definitions.note: a coin of British India, worth a sixteenth of a rupee

indicators.note: tossing turns the coin over, so the word is read the other way round
the word reads the same either way, so turning it round changes nothing

parts.note: a coin of British India, worth a sixteenth of a rupee

explanation.surface: Flipping an antique coin will not affect the outcome.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a palindrome, so flipping it round leaves it as it was.
explanation.definitionFit: This was a former Indian and Pakistani coin worth one sixteenth of a rupee.

clue.text: Poor excuse about flipping rubbish estate managers

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the shuffled excuse wraps round the other piece
a poor version of a word is a bad one, so the letters of excuse are rearranged
flipping turns the word for rubbish back to front

parts.note: rot is nonsense or rubbish

explanation.surface: Someone offers a feeble justification about some wretched garbage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor' makes EXECUS and 'flipping' makes TOR, which 'about' sets inside. 'Flipping' passes in the surface as a mild British expletive.
explanation.definitionFit: These are the people named in a will to administer the dead person's property.

clue.text: Chain up small, inebriate woman

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters are read from bottom to top

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
Edna, the Inebriate Woman is a 1971 BBC television play about a homeless alcoholic

explanation.surface: A tipsy woman is told to chain herself up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reverses S and EDNA, giving SANDE backwards. Edna, the Inebriate Woman was a well-known BBC play.
explanation.definitionFit: These form the long mountain range running down the western side of South America.

clue.text: Eating out, being sick having thrown up starter

indicators.note: having thrown up the starter means the first letter has been discarded

parts.note: retching is heaving as if to vomit

explanation.surface: After a meal at a restaurant, someone is ill and loses the first course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having thrown up starter' drops the first letter, R. 'Eating out' sounds like dining in a restaurant but means corroding.
explanation.definitionFit: This printmaking process uses acid to corrode, or eat away, lines in a metal plate.

clue.text: Apr. 8. Shot aardvark

indicators.note: shot means ruined or broken up, so these letters are scrambled

parts.note: Apr is taken as its letters, the abbreviation of April
the figure is written out as a word

explanation.surface: A diary entry: on 8 April an aardvark was shot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot' rearranges APR plus EIGHT.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an alternative name for the African burrowing mammal, from its Afrikaans name meaning earth pig.

clue.text: It could have layers of cracknel at regular intervals

indicators.note: taking letters at regular intervals means picking every other one

explanation.surface: Something layered with brittle toffee, placed evenly throughout.
explanation.walkthrough: The 1st, 3rd, 5th and 7th letters of CRACKNEL. The 9s mentioned at 17 down refer to this answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A sponge or wedding confection is often built up in tiers or sandwiched layers.

clue.text: A bit of Malbec; not all Argentinians knock it back in a single gulp!

indicators.note: to knock a drink back is to swallow it, and back also tells us to read the letters backwards
a bit of the phrase means the letters are found inside it

explanation.surface: Not every Argentinian downs a glass of Malbec in one go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A bit of' picks ECNOTALLA out of 'Malbec; not all Argentinians'; 'knock it back' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something simultaneously, in one go, matches swallowing a drink in one swig.

clue.text: Where Putin says "yes" to a cuppa?

definitions.text: Where Putin says "yes" to a cuppa?

parts.note: da is the Russian word for yes
cha is slang for tea, a cuppa

explanation.surface: The Russian president accepts the offer of a mug of tea, but where?
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes where the Russian leader might relax over tea, and also builds the word.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a Russian country house or villa, where a president might take his tea.

clue.text: Pet excuse used by student?

parts.note: a favourite excuse of a pupil whose work is not handed in, which blames a household animal

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pet excuse' means a favourite excuse, but the excuse really does involve a pet.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the proverbially lame excuse for missing coursework, blaming a household animal for destroying it.

clue.text: Spurn Point, according to Spooner, a great source of vitamin D

definitions.text: a great source of vitamin D

indicators.note: Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the first sounds of the two words are exchanged

parts.note: to spurn is to shun, to reject
to point is to sign or signal with a gesture

explanation.surface: Spurn Point, a Yorkshire headland, is said to be a sunny spot.
explanation.walkthrough: SHUN SIGN with the opening sounds swapped by sound. Spurn Point is a spit of land at the mouth of the Humber in Yorkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: Skin makes vitamin D when exposed to daylight, so sunlight is its chief natural source.

clue.text: Post office engaging worker — it's for the Xmas season

indicators.note: engaging means taking on or holding, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: an ant is a worker, the crossword stock worker insect

explanation.surface: The post office takes on seasonal staff for Christmas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'engaging' sounds like hiring staff, but it signals one piece holding the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A pantomime is a British family stage show traditionally staged around Christmas and New Year, with slapstick and audience shouting.

clue.text: Low note suggestive of frivolty in Beethoven sonata

parts.note: to low is to moo, as cattle do
light-hearted, unserious entertainment is called light

explanation.surface: A deep musical tone hints at playfulness within a piano sonata.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Low' looks musical but is the cow's call.
explanation.definitionFit: Beethoven's Piano Sonata No. 14 is popularly known by this nickname.

clue.text: Never to be forgotten, Mike's Elba/Rome trip

parts.note: Mike is M in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: a trip sets things moving or stumbling, so the letters of the two place names are jumbled

explanation.surface: Mike's holiday to Elba and Rome will live long in the memory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trip' looks like the holiday itself but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Something worth remembering, unforgettable, would never slip from memory.

clue.text: First steer hide Henry dropped in the compound

parts.note: to lead is to be first
a steer is a castrated bull, an ox

indicators.note: dropped means the letter for Henry is left out

parts.note: H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance

explanation.surface: A rancher's first bullock loses its skin in the corral.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dropped' leaves IDE. 'compound' hints at a cattle enclosure but is chemical.
explanation.definitionFit: A chemical compound of the metal Pb with oxygen, used in paints and glass.

clue.text: Thanks to Mary — she of the 9s — embracing yen for soft fruit

indicators.note: embracing means holding within, so the yen symbol goes inside

parts.note: ta is informal British for thanks
Mary Berry is the famous TV cake baker, and the answer to 9 is cake
Y is the abbreviation for the Japanese yen

explanation.surface: Gratitude to a cake-loving woman with a craving for berries.
explanation.walkthrough: Mary Berry is a British baking writer and Great British Bake Off judge, hence 'she of the 9s' (cakes).
explanation.definitionFit: This is a cross between a blackberry and a raspberry, a juicy soft fruit.

clue.text: Happy days for Godot, newly semi-retired

indicators.note: newly means made afresh, so the letters of Godot are rearranged
retired means withdrawn or gone back, so semi is read backwards

explanation.surface: Beckett's Godot, partly retired, finally enjoys his golden years.
explanation.walkthrough: 'newly' rearranges GODOT to GOODT; 'retired' turns SEMI into IMES. Happy Days is also a Beckett play.
explanation.definitionFit: A period of enjoyment and prosperity is a spell of cheerful days.

clue.text: Apprentice head over heels about music mag — deservedly so

indicators.note: about means around, so the reversed beginner wraps round the magazine
turning head over heels flips the word end to end

parts.note: a tiro is a novice or apprentice
NME, the New Musical Express, is a British music magazine

explanation.surface: A trainee falls madly for a music magazine, and rightly so.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head over heels' makes ORIT, and 'about' wraps it round the magazine. 'head over heels' reads as infatuation in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Earned on the strength of one's own ability, a selection is justified and fair.

clue.text: See 12
Toledo resident composer not a novelist

indicators.note: not means without, so the a is removed

parts.note: Edward Elgar was an English composer
Umberto Eco was an Italian novelist

explanation.surface: A Spanish townsperson is a composer rather than a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not a' drops A from ELGAR.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek-born painter settled in Toledo, Spain, and spent most of his career there.

clue.text: See 12
With which one wields the axe (that's funny!) over newspaper

definitions.text: With which one wields the axe

indicators.note: in a down clue, over puts the first piece above the second

parts.note: ha is an exclamation of amusement
FT is the Financial Times newspaper

explanation.surface: Someone laughs at axe-wielding, set over a newspaper headline.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the handle of an axe or knife, the part held to swing the tool.

clue.text: BBC boss invested in small Scottish club

indicators.note: invested in means placed inside, so the boss goes into the small word

parts.note: wee is Scottish for small
the BBC is run by its Director General, DG

explanation.surface: The head of the BBC puts money into a minor Scottish football side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'club' looks like a football team but is a golf club; 'invested in' sounds financial.
explanation.definitionFit: A golf iron with a steeply angled face, used for short lofted shots.

clue.text: Take steps to heckle Verhofstadt loudly

parts.note: to heckle a speaker is to boo

indicators.note: loudly means spoken aloud, so the result is how the words sound

parts.note: Guy Verhofstadt is a Belgian politician, the European Parliament's Brexit coordinator

explanation.surface: An MEP is jeered in parliament and is told to act.
explanation.walkthrough: Verhofstadt's first name, said aloud, gives the second syllable.
explanation.definitionFit: To dance energetically to pop music is to move your feet in rhythm.

clue.text: One formerly from the 6 stored in tin can

indicators.note: stored in means kept inside, so the letters are found within these words

explanation.surface: Someone from the mountains is preserved in a can.
explanation.walkthrough: The 6 is the answer to 6 down, the mountain range.
explanation.definitionFit: The Incas were the pre-Columbian people whose empire ran along the South American mountains.

clue.text: Terminated FBI agent being probed by the taxman in the past

indicators.note: being probed means something is pushed inside, so the taxman goes into the agent

parts.note: a Fed is an American federal agent
IR is the Inland Revenue, the former UK tax authority

explanation.surface: A US agent, investigated by tax officials, loses his job.
explanation.walkthrough: The Inland Revenue was the UK's tax collector until 2005, hence 'in the past'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being sacked or dismissed from employment means your job has been ended.

clue.text: Violent uni bovver for Jacob Rees-Mogg?

definitions.note: an example: a well-fed gentleman of refined tastes, indicated by the question mark

indicators.note: violent means wild, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Rough student trouble is just what a posh Tory would deplore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Violent' rearranges UNI BOVVER. Bovver is British slang for trouble or fighting; Jacob Rees-Mogg is a famously patrician Conservative MP.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who enjoys good food and drink and lives luxuriously, as the patrician MP is presented.

clue.text: T. May's predecessor taking on Europe following article in best-selling Florentine work

indicators.note: following places one piece after the other

parts.note: the is the definite article

indicators.note: taking on means taking in, so the European letter goes inside

parts.note: David Cameron preceded Theresa May as prime minister

explanation.surface: Cameron, Theresa May's forerunner, engages with Europe after a newspaper article.
explanation.walkthrough: The predecessor is given with his initial, D for David; 'taking on' sets Europe's E after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Boccaccio's collection of a hundred tales told by Florentines escaping the plague was a medieval bestseller.
